en: The Sūtra of Prince Sudāna, translated by the Śramaṇa Shengjian of the Western Qin under imperial decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, Nanda was seated in the midst of his fourfold assembly of disciples, together with innumerable bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
At that time, the Buddha smiled, and five-colored light issued from his mouth.
Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in reverence, knelt down on his right knee, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since I have served the Buddha for more than twenty years, I have never before seen the Buddha smile as he does today."
Does the Buddha now contemplate the Buddhas of the past, the future, and the present?
Or does he have some specific intention?
We wish to hear this.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"I do not dwell upon the Buddhas of the past, future, or present; I simply dwell upon my own practice of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) during incalculable, asankhyeya kalpas in the past."
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
“What constitutes the practice of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)?
The Buddha said:
"In the distant past, incalculable eons ago, there was a great kingdom named Yava, whose king was named Śiva.
He ruled the country with the True Dharma and did not oppress the people."
The king had four thousand ministers who governed sixty small kingdoms and eight hundred villages.
He possessed five hundred large white elephants.
The king had twenty thousand consorts, yet none of them bore him a son.
The king himself offered prayers and sacrifices to the various deities, mountains, and rivers; consequently, the consort perceived that she was pregnant.
The king personally attended to the consort’s bedding and food and drink, ensuring they were all refined and soft.
When the ten months were complete, the Crown Prince was born.
Upon hearing that the prince had been born, the twenty thousand ladies of the palace were all filled with joy and leaped for gladness; milk spontaneously flowed from their breasts.
For this reason, the prince was named Sudāna.
There were four wet nurses to care for the prince:
one to nurse him, one to carry him, one to bathe him, and one to take him out for excursions and play.
When the Prince reached the age of sixteen, he had fully mastered writing, calculation, archery, charioteering, as well as all the rites and music.
The Prince served his parents as if serving celestial deities, and the King established a separate palace for the Prince.
"Since his youth, the Prince has always delighted in practicing generosity; he wishes that all sentient beings—whether the people of the world, birds, or beasts—may constantly obtain its blessings."

Foolish people are stingy and greedy, refusing to practice giving; deluded and self-deceived, they gain no benefit for themselves. When the wise dwell in the world, they know that giving is a source of virtue.
Those who practice giving are all praised together by the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats of the past, future, and present.
"As the Prince’s years grew long, the Great King took a consort for him.
The consort’s name was Māndhātṛ; she was the daughter of a king.
She was peerless in her beauty, her body adorned with exquisite necklaces of lapis lazuli, gold, silver, and various jewels."
The Prince had a son and a daughter; the Prince thought to himself, "I wish to perform the deed of *dānapāramitā*.
The Prince then addressed the King:
"I wish to go out for a tour and observation.
The King immediately granted his permission.
Thereupon, the Prince departed from the city.
Śakra, King of Devas, descended and transformed himself into poor, deaf, blind, and mute persons, all of whom were by the side of the road.
When the Prince saw them, he immediately turned his chariot back toward the palace, filled with great sorrow and distress, finding no joy.
The King asked the Crown Prince:
"Having returned from your excursion, why are you not joyful?
The Prince replied:
"I have just been out for a stroll and saw many who were poor, destitute, deaf, blind, and mute; this is why I am sorrowful.
I wish to beg a single boon from the King; I do not know whether Your Majesty will grant me leave."
The King replied to the Prince:
"Whatever you wish to desire, it shall depend on what you seek;
I will not go against your intention."
The Prince said:

"I wish to take all the precious treasures from the royal treasury and place them outside the four city gates and within the marketplace to practice giving; whatever anyone requests, I shall not refuse their wishes."
The King said to the Crown Prince, "I grant you whatever you desire; I shall not oppose you.

Thereupon, the Crown Prince ordered his attendants to transport precious treasures in carts and place them outside the four city gates and in the marketplace to be given as alms, allowing people to take whatever they wished without opposing their desires.

Throughout the eight directions and above and below, there were none who did not hear of and know the Prince’s meritorious virtues; among the people from distant lands, there were those who came from a hundred *li*, those who came from a thousand *li*, and those who came from ten thousand *li* away.

If people desire food, he feeds them; if they desire clothing, he gives it to them; if they desire gold, silver, or precious treasures, he grants them as much as they wish, never refusing their desires in whatever they seek to obtain.
At that time, there was an enemy state and a rival who, having heard that the Prince delighted in giving and would never refuse anyone's request,
immediately assembled his ministers and various practitioners to deliberate together, saying:
"The King of the country of Yebha possesses a white elephant that walks upon lotuses, named Sudāna, which is exceedingly strong and skilled in combat."
"Whenever we engage in mutual warfare with other nations, this elephant always achieves victory.
Who among you can go and beg it [to be given]?
All the ministers replied:
"There is no one who can go and obtain it.
Among them were eight practitioners of the Way who immediately addressed the king, saying:
"We can go and beg for it."
"Please provide me with provisions.
The king immediately granted them to him.
The king then spoke to him, saying:
"Whoever can capture this elephant, I shall reward you handsomely.
The eight practitioners immediately set out with their staffs, traveling far across mountains and rivers until they reached the kingdom of Yebha.
Upon reaching the gate of the Prince’s palace, they all leaned upon their staffs and stood before the gate with one foot raised.
At that time, the gatekeeper went inside and informed the Prince:
"There are several practitioners outside, all leaning on staffs and standing with one foot raised."
He said to himself, "I have come from afar wishing to beg for something.
Upon hearing this, the Prince was greatly delighted; he went out to meet him, prostrated before him as a son would see his father, and inquired after his well-being.
“From where have you come?
Did you encounter any hardship while traveling on the road?
What do you seek to obtain that you hold up one foot in the air?”
The eight practitioners said:
"We have heard that the Crown Prince delights in giving and never refuses anyone’s request.

His name resounds throughout the eight directions, reaching upward to the azure heavens and downward to the Yellow Springs. The merit of his virtue in giving is immeasurable; from far and near, there are none who do not sing his praises or know of him."
"What people say of the Crown Prince is indeed true.
Now he is the son of gods and men; what gods and men say can never deceive.
If the Crown Prince truly is able to practice giving and does not oppose the wishes of others, we wish to beg of him the white elephant that walks upon lotuses."
The Prince then led him to the elephant stable and ordered that one elephant be taken away.
The eight Daoist masters said,
"I specifically desire to travel upon the white elephant named Sudāna, who walks upon lotus flowers."
The Prince said:
"This great white elephant is what my father, the King, holds most dear; the King regards this white elephant no differently than he does me.
I cannot give it to you."
"If I give it to you, I shall immediately lose my father the King's favor; he might even, because of this elephant, banish me from the kingdom.
The Prince then reflected to himself:
"I previously made a solemn vow that in all acts of giving, I would not oppose the wishes of others."
If I do not give it now, I would be acting contrary to my original intention.
If I do not bestow this image as a gift, how could I ever attain the unsurpassed mind of universal equanimity?
Listen, I shall give it to you, so that I may fulfill my unsurpassed mind of universal equanimity.
The Prince said:
“I agree! Very well!”
"I wish to give it to you.
He then commanded his attendants:
"Bring out the elephant with its golden saddle immediately!"
The Crown Prince took water in his left hand to wash the hands of the mendicant, while with his right hand he led the elephant and presented it to him.
Upon receiving the elephant, the eight men offered prayers of blessing for the Crown Prince; when the blessings were finished, they mounted the white elephant and departed joyfully.
The Prince said to the practitioner,
"Depart quickly!
If the King learns of this, he will pursue you and seize you."
At that time, the eight Daoist masters immediately departed in haste.

When the various ministers of the kingdom heard that the Crown Prince had given away the white elephant as alms to his enemies, they were all greatly shocked and terrified; they fell from their couches, filled with sorrow and distress, thinking to themselves:
"The state relies solely upon this elephant to repel enemy nations."
The ministers all went to inform the king:
"The Crown Prince has given away the state's defensive treasure-elephant as a gift to his enemy.
When the king heard this, he was struck with astonishment.
The minister spoke again to the king:
"It is because of this elephant that Your Majesty has now obtained the empire."
"This elephant surpasses sixty elephants in strength, yet the Crown Prince gives it away to his enemies; I fear he will lose the kingdom.
What should we do? The Prince thus bestows gifts at his own will, and the inner treasury is emptied day by day."
"I fear that the entire kingdom, along with its wives and children, will all be given away.
When the king heard these words,
he became even more deeply distressed.
The king called a minister and asked him,
"Is it certain that the crown prince gave the white elephant to his enemy?
The minister replied to the king:
"I truly gave it to him.
Upon hearing the minister's words, the king was greatly alarmed; he fell from his bed, fainted, and lost consciousness.
Cold water was sprinkled over him, and after a long while, he revived.
The twenty thousand ladies-in-waiting were likewise all unhappy.
The king consulted with his ministers, saying:
"What should be done with the crown prince?"
Among them, one minister said:
"He who entered the elephant stable on foot should have his feet cut off;
he who pulled the elephant by the hand should have his hand cut off."
"Those who look at the elephant with their eyes should have their eyes plucked out," some said;
"They should have their heads cut off," others said.
The ministers deliberated together, each speaking thus.
Upon hearing these words, the king was deeply distressed and said to his ministers, "My son greatly loves the Way and delights in giving to others; how can I forbid him and confine him?"
Among them was a high minister who resented the deliberations of the other ministers, thinking they were improper.
"The King has but this one son, whom he loves and cherishes deeply.
How can you conceive such a thought as to wish to inflict such mutilation upon him?"
The minister said to the king:

"I, your servant, also dare not cause Your Majesty to prohibit or detain the crown prince; rather, I shall drive him out of the country and place him in the wild fields and mountains for about twelve years, which will surely cause him to feel shame."
The king then followed the words of this great minister and immediately dispatched a messenger to summon and question the prince:
"Did you give the white elephant to your enemy?"
The Prince said to the King,
"I truly gave it to him.
The King asked the Prince:
"Why have you now taken my white elephant and given it to an enemy without informing me?

The Prince replied, "Previously, I made a solemn agreement with Your Majesty that I would not oppose anyone's wishes regarding whatever I might give in charity; for this reason, I did not inform Your Majesty."
The king said,
"What was previously requested were the precious treasures themselves;
what business has the white elephant with that?"
The Prince replied, "All of these are the King's possessions; why should this alone not be included among them?
The King said to the Prince:
"Leave the kingdom immediately; I shall exile you to Mount Dandaka for twelve years.
The Prince addressed the King, saying:
"I dare not disobey the Great King’s command; however, I pray that you grant me seven more days to fulfill my humble intentions before departing the kingdom."
The king said:

"It is precisely because your practice of giving was so excessive that you have emptied the treasury of my kingdom and caused me to lose this treasure that serves as a deterrent against enemies; therefore, I am banishing you."
"You may no longer remain here for another seven days of giving; depart quickly, for you are not permitted to stay.
The Prince addressed the King, saying, "I dare not disobey the Great King’s command."
"Now I possess my own private wealth; I wish to give it as alms, and only when it is exhausted shall I depart.
I dare not trouble the state treasury further.

Thus, twenty thousand ladies-in-waiting went together to the king's presence and requested that the prince be allowed to remain for seven days to practice giving before being permitted to leave the country.
The King immediately granted his permission.
The Prince then ordered his attendants to proclaim far and wide: "To all who desire wealth and goods, let them come to the palace gate and receive whatever they wish for."
Human wealth and possessions cannot be preserved forever; they will inevitably be destroyed and dispersed.
People from all quarters came to his gate, and the Prince provided them with food and drink, bestowing upon them precious jewels so that they might depart as they pleased.
When the wealth was exhausted after seven days, the poor became wealthy and the myriad people rejoiced.
The Prince said to his wife:
"Arise quickly and listen to my words."
"Great King, he has now driven me away to dwell in Mount Dandaka for twelve years.
Upon hearing the Prince's words, the Queen started in alarm and rose, saying to him:
"What transgression have I committed that the King should treat me so?"
The Prince replied,
"Because my acts of giving were so extreme, I have emptied the state treasury and bestowed the noble white elephant upon my enemies.
For this reason, the King and his ministers have become incensed and are pursuing me together."

Manḍī said: "If the kingdom is to be prosperous and overflowing, I wish that the Great King, along with all your ministers, officials, and citizens, great and small, may enjoy boundless wealth and happiness; we need only strive together in this mountain to diligently seek the Way."
The Prince said:
"When a person is in the mountains, in a place of terror, it is difficult to maintain a steady mind.
Tigers, wolves, and fierce beasts are truly fearsome."
"You are accustomed to the pleasures of Kauśāmbī; how can you endure this?

While you were in the palace, your garments were fine and soft, your quarters were curtained and draped, and your food and drink were sweet and delicious, provided according to every whim of the palate."
Now, when you lie in the mountains, you sleep upon mats of grass; when you eat, you consume fruits and gourds.
How can you find pleasure in this?
Furthermore, there are frequent winds, rains, thunder, lightning, mists, and dew that cause one's hair to stand on end.
In cold it is bitterly cold; in heat it is intensely hot.
One cannot rely upon the spaces between trees, moreover, the ground is strewn with thorns, gravel, stones, and venomous insects—how can you endure such things?
Manjī said: "How could I use these fine, soft curtains and delicious foods for myself while parting from the Prince?
I can never bear to be separated from him."
"I shall surely go along with the Prince.
A king takes his banner as his mark; fire takes its smoke as its mark; a woman takes her husband as her mark; I rely solely upon the Prince."
"The Crown Prince is my deity.
When the Crown Prince was in the kingdom, he bestowed alms upon people from the four quarters, and I always shared in those acts with him.
Now that the Crown Prince has gone far away, if someone comes to beg, how should I respond?"
"When I hear that someone has come to seek the Crown Prince, I shall surely die of grief; of this there is no doubt.
The Prince said, "I am fond of practicing generosity and do not oppose the wishes of others. If someone comes to me begging for my son or my daughter, I cannot but give them to him."
"If you do not comply with my words, you will disturb my virtuous mind; therefore, you must not go.
Manjī said, "I shall listen and follow wherever the Prince bestows his gifts without weariness; there has never been one in this world whose generosity equals that of the Prince."
The Prince said, "If you can do so,
it is most excellent. Then the Prince,
together with his consort and their two sons, went to his mother's place to take leave before departing, and addressed his mother, saying:
"I pray that you will frequently admonish the Great King to govern the country with the True Dharma, and not oppress or wrong the people.
When the mother heard the Crown Prince’s words of farewell, she was moved by deep sorrow and grief.
She spoke to those standing nearby, saying:
"My body is like stone and my heart is as hard as tempered iron; in serving the Great King, I have never committed a transgression.
Now that my only son has abandoned me and departed, how could my heart not shatter and cause me to die?"
"While the child was in my womb, he grew day and night like the leaves of a tree; now that the son has grown to maturity, he has abandoned me and departed.
All the other queens will surely rejoice, for our King will no longer show me respect."
"If Heaven does not oppose my wish, it shall cause my son to return to the kingdom swiftly.
The Prince, together with his consort and their two children, performed a prostration before his parents and then departed.
"Twenty thousand ladies each gave a string of pearls to the Prince, and four thousand ministers presented him with flowers made of the seven precious gems.

As the Prince departed from the inner palace toward the north gate of the city, he bestowed all the precious gem-encrusted flowers upon the people from the four quarters; they were immediately exhausted."
The officials and commoners, numbering several million of all ages who had accompanied the Crown Prince on his journey, all spoke among themselves in secret:
"The Crown Prince is a virtuous man; he is the deity of this kingdom."
"How could our parents ever drive away such a precious son?
Those who witnessed it all grieved for him together.
The Prince sat beneath a tree outside the city and took leave of those who had come to see him off, saying, "You may return from here."
The officials and citizens, both old and young, returned home shedding tears.
The Prince, together with his consort and two sons, rode in the carriage and drove it himself; having traveled some distance, he halted beneath a tree to rest.
A Brahmin came to beg for a horse, and the Prince immediately unharnessed the carriage and gave the horse to him.
He placed his two children in the carriage; the Consort pushed from behind while he himself entered the shafts and pulled it along by hand.
Just as he proceeded further, he again encountered a brahmin coming to beg for his chariot;
the Prince immediately gave him the chariot.
Just as he proceeded further, he again encountered a brahmin coming to beg.
The Prince said,
"I have nothing that I cherish enough to give to you;
my wealth and possessions are all exhausted."
The brāhmaṇa said,
"If you have no wealth, give me the garment upon your body.
The prince immediately removed his precious robe and gave it to him, putting on an old garment in its place.
As he proceeded further, he again encountered a brāhmaṇa who came to beg.
The prince gave his consort’s garments to him.
Continuing on his way, he again encountered a brāhmaṇa who came to beg.
The Prince gave his two children’s clothes to him.
Having completely exhausted his gifts of chariots, horses, money, and clothing, he felt not even a hair’s breadth of regret.
The Prince carried his son upon his own back, while the Consort carried their daughter; they departed on foot.
The Prince, the Consort, and their two children followed one another into the mountains with serene countenances and joyful hearts.
"The Mount Dantaka is over six thousand *li* from the kingdom of Yebha.
Being so far from the kingdom, he traveled through vast wildernesses and suffered greatly from hunger and thirst.
Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, immediately manifested within that desolate wilderness a city with its walls, markets, streets, and alleys, along with music, clothing, food, and drink."
A person from within the city came out to welcome the Prince, saying, "You may stay here for a while to eat, drink, and enjoy yourself.
The Consort said to the Prince, "The journey has been most arduous; might you not find it convenient to rest here?"
The Prince said:
"My father the King has banished me to Mount Dantaka; to remain here would be to disobey my father's command, and such a person is no filial son."
He then departed from the city; looking back at the city, it suddenly vanished. Continuing further on his journey, he arrived at Mount Dantaka.
At the foot of the mountain was a great body of water so deep that it could not be crossed.
The consort said to the Prince: "We should stay here for now; we must wait until the water recedes before crossing."
The Crown Prince said:
"My father the King has exiled me to Mount Dantaka; to dwell here would be to disobey my father’s command, and I would not be a filial son."

The Prince immediately entered the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind, whereupon a great mountain appeared in the water to dam it; the Prince then waded across with his consort, lifting their robes above the water.
Having crossed over, the Prince immediately thought to himself:
"If I depart as I am, the water will flood and drown the people and all crawling and flying creatures.
The Prince then turned back and addressed the water, saying:
"Let the water flow back as it was before;
if there are those who wish to come to my place, let them all be able to cross.
As soon as the Prince had finished speaking, the water immediately flowed back as it was before.

"Previously, when he arrived at Mount Dantaka, the Prince saw the mountain’s precipitous peaks and towering crags; the trees were lush and thick, and hundreds of birds sang mournfully. There were flowing springs and clear ponds with sweet waters and delicious fruits, and a great variety of exotic creatures, including wild ducks, geese, cormorants, kingfishers, and mandarin ducks."
The Prince said to his consort:

"Behold these trees in the mountains reaching toward the heavens, none of them broken or injured; they drink from this beautiful spring and eat these sweet fruits, and within these mountains there are also those who practice the Way."
"When the Prince entered the mountains, the birds and beasts therein were all filled with great joy and came forth to welcome him.
On the mountain there was a practitioner named Ājīvaka, five hundred years of age, who possessed most wondrous virtue."
The Prince performed a prostration, withdrew to stand aside, and said:
"In these mountains, where is there a pleasant place with fine sweet fruits and spring water where we may stay?
Āṭavika replied:
"This mountain is entirely a land of merit; it is a place where one may dwell.
The practitioner then said, "This mountain is a place of purity; how can you bring your wife and children here, intending to study the Way?"
Before the Prince had replied, Māndhātṛ asked the practitioner,
"How many years have you been practicing the Way here?
The practitioner answered:
"I have dwelt in these mountains for four or five hundred years.
Manthāṭī said to him,
"For one who calculates in terms of 'self,' 'person,' and 'individual,' when will they ever attain the Way?"
"Though you have long been in the mountains, you are no different from the trees.
Only by not reckoning 'self,' 'person,' or 'individual' can one attain the Way.
The practitioner said:
"I truly do not know of this matter.
The Prince then asked the practitioner,
"Have you perhaps heard of the Prince of the King of Yebao, Sudāna?"
The practitioner said,
"I have heard of it many times, but I have never seen it.
The Prince said:
"I am indeed Prince Sudāna.
The practitioner asked the prince,
"What is it that you seek?"
The Prince replied,
"I wish to seek the Mahāyāna path.
The man of the Way said:
"The merit of the Prince is such that he will attain the Mahāyāna path before long.
When the Prince attains the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path, I shall become his foremost disciple in spiritual powers (ṛddhi)."

The practitioner immediately pointed out the place where the prince was staying; thereupon, the prince followed the practitioner’s example by binding his hair into a topknot and wearing matted locks, subsisting on spring water, fruits, and melons as his food and drink.
He immediately gathered firewood and constructed a small grass hut, and for both Mantharā and his two young sons, he built one grass hut each, making three huts in total.
The son was named Yari; at seven years of age, he wore garments of grass and followed his father in and out.
The girl was named Kinnarā; she was six years old and wore a garment of deer skin as she followed her mother in and out.
All the birds and beasts of the mountains were filled with joy and attached themselves to the Prince.

"As soon as the Prince stayed there for one night, springs welled up from all the empty pools in the mountains; withered trees and all the other plants sprouted flowers and leaves; all venomous insects and beasts were extinguished, and those that used to devour one another now ate grass of their own accord; various fruit trees flourished spontaneously, and a hundred birds warbled together in harmonious, mournful song."
Manjī was primarily responsible for gathering fruit to feed the Prince and his two children.
The two boys also left their parents and went about playing with birds and beasts by the water’s edge, sometimes staying there overnight.
At that time, the boy Yari was playing on a lion cub; the lion leaped and lunged, causing Yari to fall to the ground and injure his face, from which blood flowed.
The monkey then took leaves from a tree to wipe the blood from his face and led him to the water’s edge to wash it.
The Crown Prince was also seated there and saw them from afar, saying, "Even among birds and beasts, such a heart exists.
At that time, in the kingdom of Kuru, there was a poor brāhmaṇa who married at the age of forty; his wife was exceedingly beautiful.
The brahmins have twelve deformities: their bodies are black as lacquer;

they have three warts on their faces; their noses are perfectly flat; both eyes are blue; their faces are wrinkled and their lips are pendulous; they stammer in speech; they have large bellies and protruding hips; their legs are twisted; their heads are bald and shaggy; and their appearance resembles that of a ghost.
His wife detested the sight of him and cast spells, wishing for his death.
While she was out fetching water, she encountered several young men who mocked her husband’s appearance and ridiculed him, asking:
"You are so exceptionally handsome; how could you be the wife of such a man?"
The wife said to the young man:
"This old man's head is white like frost upon a tree;
morning and evening I wish for him to die, but what can I do when he refuses to die?"
The wife then took the water and wept as she returned home, saying to her husband:
"Just now while I was fetching water, a group of young men made lewd advances toward me; you must find me some male and female slaves."
"If I have male and female slaves, I shall no longer have to draw water myself, and people will no longer mock me.
Her husband said, "I am extremely poor; where could I possibly obtain male and female slaves?"
The wife said:
"If you do not seek out slaves for me, I shall depart and no longer live with you.
Thus spoke the wife.
"I have often heard that because Prince Sudāna’s practice of giving was so extreme, his father the King banished him to Mount Dandaka.
He has a son and a daughter; you may go there to beg for them."
The husband said, "Mount Tandan is more than six thousand li from here; I have never traveled by mountain path before, so where shall I seek it?
The wife said:
"If you do not seek out slaves for me, I shall take my own life by stabbing myself to death.
Her husband said,
"I would rather kill my own body than allow you to die."
The husband said,
"If you wish me to go, you must provide me with provisions for the journey.
The wife said:
"Go then, but you have no provisions.
The Brahmin prepared his own provisions and set out on the road.
Thereupon, the Brahmin traveled directly to the kingdom of Yebha; arriving outside the gates of the royal palace, he asked the gatekeeper:
"Where is Prince Mahāsattva now?
At that time, the gatekeeper entered and informed the king:
"A brāhmaṇa has come outside asking for the prince."
When the king heard that someone was seeking the crown prince, his heart was moved with both grief and anger, and he said:
"It is solely because of these people that they have driven away my son.
Has this person come here again?"
The king then spoke this parable himself:
"It is like a fire that blazes of its own accord, yet is further augmented by the addition of fuel.
Now my grief and anxiety are like the blazing fire, and people coming to inquire after the prince are like adding fuel to it."
The Brahmin said:

"I have come from afar, having heard the name of the Prince, which reaches upward to the azure heavens and downward to the Yellow Springs. Since the Prince’s acts of giving do not oppose the wishes of others, I have come from afar desiring to obtain something."
The king said, “The crown prince dwells alone in the deep mountains and is in great poverty; what could he possibly give to you?
The brahmin replied:
"The Prince has nothing at all, yet he wishes to see you.
The King then dispatched a man to show him the way.
The Brahmin immediately set out for Mount Dantaka; upon reaching the edge of a great body of water, he simply focused his mind on the Prince and was able to cross over.
Then the brahmin entered the mountains and encountered a hunter, whom he asked:
"While you are in these mountains, have you perhaps seen Prince Mahāsattva?"

The hunter, who already knew that the Prince had been moved to the mountains because he sat in meditation after giving alms to the Brahmins, then seized the Brahmin, bound him to a tree, and whipped him with a cudgel until his body was completely torn apart.
He reviled him, saying:
"I wish to shoot you in the belly and devour your flesh; what is the use of asking about the prince?
The Brahmin thought to himself:
"Should I now be killed by my own son?
I shall simply utter a deceptive word. He then said:
"Should you not question me? The hunter asked,
"What do you wish to say?"
The Brahmin said,
"Because the royal father longs to see the crown prince, he has sent me to summon him back to the kingdom.
The hunter immediately released him and offered his apologies:
"I truly did not know him," he replied,
and immediately pointed out the place.
The brahmin then went directly to the Prince's location.
When the Prince saw the brahmin approaching from afar, he was filled with great joy and welcomed him by paying his respects;
he then inquired after him, saying: "Whence have you come?"
"Are you not weary from traveling?
What do you seek?
The brahmin replied:
"I have come from afar; my entire body aches and I am greatly hungry and thirsty.
The Prince immediately invited the Brahmin to enter and sit, then brought forth fruits, melons, water, and juices and placed them before him.
When the brahmin had finished drinking water and eating fruit, he spoke to the prince, saying:
"I am a man from the kingdom of Kuru. I have long heard that you, Prince, delight in practicing generosity and that your fame has spread throughout the ten directions."
"I am extremely poor and wish to beg something from the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince said,
"I have nothing that I would give to you."
"I have given away everything I possess; there is nothing left with which to give you.
The brahmin said, "If you have no goods, give me your two sons to serve as attendants, so that they may support you in your old age."
Thus he spoke three times.
The Prince said:
"You have come from afar for this purpose, desiring my son and daughter; how can I not grant them to you?"
At that time, while the two boys were playing, the Prince called out to them, saying:
"A brahmin has come from afar to beg for you; I have already granted him your permission.
You should go with him."
The two children ran into their father’s armpits, weeping as they said, "We have seen many Brahmins before, but never one such as this.
This is no Brahmin; he is merely a ghost."
"Now my mother has gone to gather fruit and has not yet returned, while my father has taken me to serve as food for a ghost; my death is certain, beyond doubt.
When my mother returns and cannot find me, she will surely weep and wail in grief and sorrow, like a cow searching for her calf."
The Prince said,
"I have already given my word to him.
How can I withdraw it?"
"He is merely a brahmin, not a ghost; he will certainly not devour you.
You may go after him.
The brahmin said:
"I wish to depart, but I fear that if her mother comes, I shall no longer be able to go.
You have maintained a virtuous heart toward me; were her mother to come, she would surely destroy your good intention."
The Prince replied, "Since my birth, I have never once regretted an act of giving.
The Prince then washed the Brahmin’s hands with water, took his two children by the hand, and bestowed them upon him; at that moment, the earth shook.
The two boys were unwilling to follow him; they returned to their father, knelt prostrately before him, and said to him:
"What transgression have we committed in our past lives that we must now encounter such suffering as this—to become slaves to others, even though we are of royal lineage?"

Confess your transgressions to your father; through these causes and conditions, your offenses shall be extinguished and merit shall arise, so that in every lifetime you may never again encounter such [suffering].
The Prince said to his son:
‘All affectionate attachments in the world must end in separation; since all things are impermanent, how can they be preserved?’”
"When I have attained the unsurpassed path of equality, I shall deliver you myself.
The two sons said to their father, "Please convey our thanks to our mother;
from this moment on we are forever parted, and though it is regrettable that we cannot bid her farewell in person, we must endure this suffering as the result of our own past karmic offenses."
"I think of my mother, who will suffer grief, sorrow, and exhaustion at having lost me.
The Brahmin said, "I am old and frail;
when the young children each abandon me and run to their own mothers, how could I possibly catch them?"
"You must bind them and hand them over to me.
The Prince then took the two boys by their hands and had the Brahmin bind them himself, tying them together so that they were linked, holding the end of the rope.
The two boys refused to go with him; he whipped them with a cane until blood flowed onto the ground.
When the Prince saw this, tears fell from his eyes to the earth, causing the ground to boil.
The Crown Prince and all the birds and beasts escorted the two children; only when they were no longer in sight did they return.
All the birds and beasts followed the Crown Prince back to the place where the children had been playing; there, they cried out and rolled about, throwing themselves to the ground.
The brahmin took the two children away directly.
On the road, the children wrapped their ropes around a tree and refused to follow, hoping for their mother to come.
The brahmin whipped them with a cane.
The two children said, "Do not strike us anymore; we shall leave of our own accord.
They looked up to heaven and cried out:
"May the mountain deities and tree deities take pity on me for a moment.
I am now about to depart for a distant land to become a slave; I cannot bear to part from my mother.
Please tell my mother to cast aside her fruit and come quickly so that we may meet."
In the mountains, the mother felt an itch beneath her left foot, her right eye twitched, and milk flowed from both breasts.
She then reflected to herself:
"Never before have I experienced such a marvel."
"What shall I do with these fruits?
It would be best to return and look after my son, lest some misfortune befall him.
Having said this, he abandoned the fruits and returned home.

At that time, Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, knowing that the Prince had given his child to another, feared that the Queen might ruin his virtuous resolve; he then transformed himself into a lion and crouched across the path.

The consort said to the lion, "You are the king among beasts, and I am likewise a princess among men; since we are together in these mountains, I pray that you will yield a little so that I may pass by."
"I have two sons, both still very young; they have had nothing to eat since morning and are merely waiting for me.
Knowing that the brahmin was now far away, the lion rose and stepped aside to let his consort pass.
When the consort returned, she saw the Prince sitting alone and did not see her two children.

She went into their grass hut to search for them but could not find them; she went further into the children’s room to look for them but could not find them; she went to the water’s edge where the children usually played, yet they were still nowhere to be seen. She saw only the deer, roe, lions, and monkeys with whom they had played, all throwing themselves before Manjī, wailing and crying out, while the pond where they had played had completely run dry.
Mandī then returned to the place where the Prince was and asked him,
"Where are the two children?
The Prince did not answer.
Manjī spoke again:
"The child saw me from afar carrying fruit as I ran toward him; he rushed to me, fell to the ground, rose up again, and leaped about, crying out, 'Mother has come back to see me!'"
"When we sat together, they were always at my side; whenever they saw dust upon my body, they would brush it away for me.
Now I do not see my son, nor does he come to cling to me; to whom shall I give him?"
"Now that I do not see him, my heart is torn asunder.
Tell me his whereabouts at once; do not drive me to madness.
Thus he spoke three times, but the Prince did not respond.
Mantharā became even more distressed and said,
"It is still bearable that I do not see my two children, but the Prince's lack of response makes me utterly bewildered and distraught.
The Prince spoke, saying:
"A brahmin from the kingdom of Kuru has come and asked me for my two children; I have already given them to him.
When the consort heard the prince’s words, she was so overcome with grief that she fell to the ground like the collapse of Mount Tai, rolling about and weeping uncontrollably.
The Prince said:
"Stop for a moment.
Do you recognize our original vow from the time of the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara?"
At that time, I was the son of a brahmin named Vaidheya, and you were the daughter of a brahmin named Sūdarā.

You held seven stalks of flowers, while I held five hundred silver coins; I wished to buy the flowers from you to scatter them over the Buddha. You entrusted two stalks of flowers to me to offer to the Buddha, and as you did so, you made this aspiration:
"I vow that in a future life I shall always be your wife, never parting from you whether in prosperity or in adversity.
At that time, I made this solemn promise to you:
"One who wishes to be my wife must follow my will; in whatever I give as alms, she must not oppose the intentions of others, with the sole exception of not giving away her parents."
"As for all other gifts, they were entirely according to my will.
You replied to me at that time, "Yes.
Now, by giving away your child, do you instead disturb my virtuous mind?

When the consort heard the Prince’s words, her mind was opened and she recognized her past lives; she consented to follow the Prince in his acts of giving so that he might swiftly attain what his heart desired.
When Śakra, the King of Devas, saw the Prince’s such generosity, he descended to test him, wishing to know what it was he sought.
He transformed himself into a Brahmin who likewise possessed twelve deformities; arriving before the Prince, he spoke of his own accord:
"I have often heard that the Prince delights in giving and never refuses the requests of those who come seeking; therefore I have come here, wishing to beg for your consort."
The Prince said,
"Excellent!
Your Majesty may indeed obtain her."
The consort said,
"Now that you give me away to another, who will provide for the Prince?
The Prince said:
"If you do not give her now, from what source could you achieve the unsurpassed mind of equal liberation?
The Prince washed the Brahmin's hand with water, took his consort by the hand, and gave her to him.
Śākyamuni knew that the Prince was entirely without regret; the various devas praised his goodness, and heaven and earth shook greatly.
Then the brahmin took the consort away, but after walking seven paces, he immediately brought her back to entrust her to the Prince, saying:
"Do not give her to anyone else."
The Prince said:
"Why do you not take it?
Could there be anything unwholesome about it?"
Among all the wives of men, this woman is the most virtuous.
She is the only daughter of the Prince of the State, her father’s sole offspring.
For my sake, this woman threw herself into boiling water and fire; she ate coarse and poor food without ever avoiding it; she was diligent in her duties, and her countenance is upright and beautiful.
"If you take it now, my heart will rejoice.
The brahmin said to the prince, "I am not a brahmin;
I am Śakra, the Heavenly King, and have come here merely to test you."
"What do you desire?
He then resumed his form as a Śākya prince, handsome and most exquisite.
The consort immediately prostrated herself and requested three boons from him:
"First, cause the Brahmin to take my two children back and sell them in his own country;
second, ensure that my two children do not suffer from hunger and thirst."
"Thirdly, may I and the crown prince be granted an early return to our kingdom.
King Śakra said, "It shall be as you wish."
The Prince said:
"I pray that all sentient beings may attain liberation and be freed from the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Śakra, King of Devas, replied:
"Great indeed is your aspiration, lofty and unsurpassed!
If you wish to be born in heaven as the sovereign of the sun and moon, or to serve as a lord of the world with extended longevity, I can grant these to you just as you have described."
"He is most honored in the three realms; he is not one whom I can equal.
The Prince said:
"For now, I wish that I may attain great wealth, and that my constant delight in giving shall be even greater than before."
"I pray that my father, the King, and all his ministers may wish to see me.
Śakra, the Heavenly King, replied,
"It shall surely be as you wish."
In a mere moment, he suddenly vanished.
When the Brahmin of Kuru returned home with his son, his wife greeted him with abuse:
"How can you bear to bring back such a face as this?"

"This child is of royal lineage, yet he lacks a heart of compassion; he has beaten me until sores broke out and my body is covered in pus and blood. Take him quickly to sell him, and seek someone else who can be employed."
The husband followed his wife’s words and immediately went to sell him.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, traveled there and caused the marketplace to collapse, saying:
"This child is precious; no one is able to buy him."
Just as the child became hungry and thirsty, the deva used natural breath to satisfy him with fullness.
The Heavenly King transformed his mind and led him to the kingdom of Yebha.

The ministers and people of the country recognized him as the son of the Crown Prince and the grandson of the Great King; from the highest officials to the commoners, there was none in the entire land who did not grieve.
The ministers immediately asked,
"From where did you obtain this child?
The Brahmin replied:
"I obtained this by begging for myself; why do you question me?
The ministers replied, "Since you have come to enter our kingdom, we ought to question you as well."
The ministers and the people then sought to seize the brahmin’s son, but among them was an elder who admonished them, saying:
"This is the extent to which the Prince’s heart of giving has reached; if we were now to seize him, would that not be a stubborn violation of the Prince’s original intention?"
"It would be better to inform the King.
If the King learns of this, he will surely redeem him himself.
Thereupon, they desisted.
The ministers addressed the king, saying, "Great King, your two grandsons have now been sold by a brahmin.
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly alarmed; he immediately summoned the brahmin and ordered him to bring the children into the palace.
The king, together with his consort, the various ministers, and the ladies of the inner palace, saw the two children from afar and could not help but choke back their sobs.
The king asked the brahmin,
"By what means did you obtain these children?"
The brāhmaṇa replied,
“I obtained them by begging from the crown prince.
The king called his two sons and wished to embrace them, but both wept and refused to go to him for an embrace.
The king asked the brahmin,
"How much money do you require for the sale of your son?
Before the brahmin could reply, the boy spoke:
"A man shall pay one thousand silver coins and one hundred oxen;
a woman shall pay two thousand gold coins and two hundred cows.
Thus spoke the king.
"A man is what people prize; why then is the male lowly while the female is noble? The child replied, "The ladies-in-waiting in the inner palace have no kinship with the king;

some come from humble origins and others are merely maidservants, yet when they catch the king's fancy, they immediately attain high status and honor, wearing precious garments and partaking of food of a hundred flavors."

The king had an only son, yet he banished him to the deep mountains while daily indulging himself with the palace ladies; he showed no thought at all for his son, thereby making it clear that men are held in contempt while women are esteemed.
When the king heard these words, he was moved with profound sorrow; his tears flowed profusely as he said, "I have wronged you.
For what reason did you not come to my embrace?"
"Are you angry with me?
Or do you fear the brahmins?
The boy replied:
"I do not dare resent the Great King, nor do I fear the Brahmin.
In the past I was the grandson of the Great King, but now I am a human slave.
How could a human slave venture to embrace a king?"
"Therefore, we did not dare.
When the king heard his sons' words, his grief increased all the more; he immediately paid the brahmins as requested.
He called the two boys again to embrace him, and the two boys went to him at once.
The king took his two grandsons in his arms, rubbed and stroked their bodies, and asked the two boys:
"When your father was in the mountains, what did he eat and drink?
What were his clothes like?"
The two children replied:
"We eat fruits, gourds, and vegetables, and wear coarse cloth as our clothing.
We take delight in one another like the various birds, and we have no heart for sorrow or anxiety."
The king immediately sent the brāhmaṇa away.
The son addressed the king, saying:
"This brāhmaṇa is suffering greatly from hunger and thirst; I pray that you grant him a meal."
The king said,
"Are you not indignant?
For what reason do you again seek food?"
The son said, "My father loves the Way and has no further wealth or goods with which to practice giving; therefore, give me away in alms, for then I shall be my master."
I have not yet been able to serve as his messenger to fulfill my father’s spiritual intent.
How can I now bear to see him suffering from hunger and thirst without a heart of compassion?
My father has already given me away to the Brahmin; how could Your Majesty begrudge him a single meal?
The king immediately bestowed food upon the brahmin.
When the brahmin had finished eating, he returned with joy.
The king then dispatched a messenger to swiftly welcome the prince back.
The messenger received his instructions and went to welcome the Prince, but he was obstructed by water and could not cross; however, as soon as he thought of the Prince, he was able to pass through.
By the King's command, he addressed the Prince:
"You should return to the kingdom with all haste."
The King thought of seeing the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince replied,
"Your Majesty has exiled me to the mountains, with a term of twelve years."
"One year still remains; when the term is fulfilled, you shall naturally return.
The messenger returned and reported this to the king.
The king then composed another letter to give to the prince:
"You are a wise person; you should endure it when he leaves and you should endure it when he returns.
Why do you harbor resentment and not let him go?
We shall eat and drink only when we have you."
The messenger again carried the letter back; upon receiving it, the Prince placed his head to the ground in salutation, circumambulated it seven times, and then opened it to read.

Hearing that the Prince was about to return, the various birds and beasts of the mountains leaped, rolled, threw themselves down, and wailed; the mountain springs ran dry, the beasts ceased to suckle their young, and all the hundred birds cried out in sorrow, because they had lost the Prince.
The Crown Prince immediately donned his robes and returned with the consort.

Hearing that the Crown Prince was returning, the enemy state and its vengeful foe dispatched a messenger who prepared a white elephant adorned with a saddle and bridle of gold and silver; they filled a golden bowl with silver grain and a silver bowl with golden grain, and went out to meet him on the road to escort the Crown Prince back.
He apologized and expressed regret, saying:
"My previous request for the white elephant was due to my foolishness.
Because of me, the Prince has been exiled to a distant land."
Now that we have heard you are returning, our hearts are filled with joy.
We now offer back this white elephant to the Prince, along with the gold and silver grain; we pray that you will graciously accept them to absolve us of our transgressions.
The Prince replied:

"Suppose there were a person who prepared food of a hundred flavors and offered it specifically to someone; if that person, having eaten it, vomited it onto the ground, would it still be fragrant and pure enough to be eaten again?"
Now my act of giving is like spitting out; I shall never take it back again.
Mount the elephant quickly and return, to offer your apologies to the King of your country.
You have troubled yourself as an envoy, coming from afar to inquire after me with such courtesy.
Thereupon, the messenger immediately mounted the elephant and returned, reporting these matters to the king.
Because of this elephant, the enemies and adversaries of the rival kingdom were transformed into beings of kindness and benevolence.
The king and the entire assembly all conceived the aspiration for supreme, impartial liberation.
The father-king mounted an elephant to go out and welcome the crown prince; the prince then stepped forward, prostrated himself with his head at the king's feet, and returned home with him.
The people within the kingdom were all filled with joy; they scattered flowers, burned incense, hung silken banners and canopies, and sprinkled fragrant liquid upon the ground to await the Prince.
Upon entering the palace, the Prince went immediately before his mother, prostrated himself with his head at her feet, and inquired after her well-being.

The King entrusted the treasure store to the Crown Prince, who then practiced giving at will with even greater intensity than before; through unceasing generosity, he brought himself to the attainment of Buddhahood.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Such was the manner of my practice of giving when I was in a former life."
The Prince Sudāna was myself;
the father-king at that time is my present father, Śuddhodana;
and the mother at that time is the present Māyā.
The consort at that time was none other than the present Gopī;
the mountain ascetic Ājīvaka was Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
and the celestial king Śakra was Śāriputra.
The hunter at that time was Ānanda.
The boy Yari at that time is now my son Rāhula.
The girl Kṣemā at that time is now the Arhat Mālikāmātṛ.
The brahmin beggar of that time was none other than Devadatta;
the brahmin’s wife was Cañcāmāṇavikā.
Thus he underwent such hardships for incalculable kalpas, and likewise performed wholesome deeds for incalculable kalpas.
"You should uphold this sutra and preach it to all the śramaṇas; thus does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) through such generosity.
— *The Sutra of Prince Sudāna*
